contract.settlement_definition: Eight Summer League series, all with sampled rules. Game level: KXNBASUMMERGAME (named team wins the game), KXNBASUMMERSPREAD (named team wins by more than X.5), KXNBASUMMERTOTAL (combined points above X.5), KXNBASUMMER1HSPREAD and KXNBASUMMER1HTOTAL (same forms on first-half points) and KXNBASUMMER1HWINNER (team scoring more points in the first half of regulation; equal points make all team strikes No and the Tie strike Yes; postponed games stay open until the rescheduled game ends within two weeks). Event level: KXNBASUMMER (named team wins the 2026 Summer League championship) and KXNBASUMMERMVP (named player wins the Summer League MVP award). Only the 1H winner text speaks to ties and postponement; the game, spread and total texts say nothing about overtime, ties, cancellation or the result source, and the MVP text names no voting body or co-winner rule.

rules_evidence.quote: If Zuby Ejiofor wins the Pro Basketball Summer League Most Valuable Player award in the 2026 season, then the market resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: The MVP series settles on the official award, so the outcome is a selection by whoever votes (not stated), driven by individual production and team success in the event.

rules_evidence.quote: If the teams collectively score more than 199.5 points in the Golden State vs Memphis Pro Basketball Summer League game originally scheduled for Jul 19, 2026, then the market resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: Game total is combined points against a half-point strike; the text does not say whether overtime points count.

rules_evidence.quote: If both teams score the same amount of points during the half, all team strikes resolve to No and the Tie strike resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: First-half winner is a three-way partition with an explicit Tie strike, so the integer tie mass of the half margin is priced directly.

rules_evidence.quote: If Memphis wins the Golden State vs Memphis Pro Basketball Summer League game originally scheduled for Jul 19, 2026, then the market resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: Game-winner contract on a single Summer League game; no tie leg, so the game must produce a winner under the event's overtime format.

rules_evidence.quote: If Washington wins the 2026 Pro Basketball Summer League championship, then the market resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: Champion contract settles on the tournament championship, a function of group-stage seeding and single-elimination knockout games.

variants_and_edge_cases: Overtime: the game, spread and total texts are silent; Summer League overtime formats differ from regulation NBA overtime, so whether and how OT points enter KXNBASUMMERTOTAL and KXNBASUMMERSPREAD is unverified, while first-half contracts are unaffected.
First-half winner has a Tie strike (team strikes resolve No on equal points); first-half spread and total use half-point strikes, so no push.

Multiple events exist (Las Vegas, California Classic, Salt Lake City) with different participating teams and formats; the sampled game contracts are dated Jul 19, 2026, during the Las Vegas event, which also hosts the championship.
Champion (KXNBASUMMER) depends on seeding rules (record, point-differential tiebreak) as well as team strength, and teams that miss the knockout play consolation games with weaker incentives.

MVP (KXNBASUMMERMVP): the award is decided around the championship game and usually goes to a high-usage player on a team that reaches the final rounds; a player shut down early cannot win, and the text gives no rule for co-MVPs.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official Summer League box scores and period scores (NBA.com) for game and first-half series, the tournament bracket for the champion and the league announcement for the MVP; the sampled texts name no source agency.

mechanism.summary: Summer League outcomes are produced by rosters and decisions rather than by franchise strength: who actually plays (rookies, two-way and G League players, returning bench players), how long each plays under coach evaluation plans, how good those players are on a common scale given thin or non-NBA data, and a game environment (format, pace, defensive intensity) that differs from the regular season. The outcome distribution has large variance because rotations are fluid, defense and execution are loose, and teams sometimes prioritize evaluation over winning; incentives change with the tournament state. Information is scarce and arrives game-day through announcements rather than structured injury reports, which makes timing as important as level for any model.

stages.name: Roster and participation decisions
stages.description: The first stage is who is on the floor: drafted rookies, two-way players, returning bench players on contracts, G League invitees. A top pick may play one game then be shut down, and veterans sit once their evaluation is done. Announcements arrive game-day through informal channels and are the main information.
stages.distribution: Discrete participation states with team-policy-driven probabilities; high-impact players have a bimodal minutes distribution (full or zero).

stages.name: Coach minutes plans and rotations
stages.description: Coaches use Summer League to evaluate players, so minutes are allocated to give looks to all players rather than to maximize winning; rookies often have caps and second-round or two-way players receive extended minutes. Rotation patterns are less stable than in the regular season and are set by program philosophy.
stages.distribution: Plan-driven minute vectors with random deviations; minutes variance within player is high and cross-team variation is structural.

stages.name: Team strength from translated talent
stages.description: A team's Summer League strength is the minutes-weighted sum of players' strengths on a common scale. With limited NBA data for most participants, ratings must be translated from college, G League and international performance and drafted position, with large uncertainty and no cohesion effect from shared practice.
stages.distribution: Sum of independent uncertain player ratings; strength uncertainty large (assumed prior sd of team rating of 5-8 points per 100 possessions, unsourced) and heavy-tailed because of star presence.

stages.name: Game environment: format, pace and variance
stages.description: The format (period length, overtime rules, foul limits) and talent mix produce a different scoring environment: more possessions per minute, weaker half-court defense and larger point-total variance. League-specific baselines are required, and event-level differences exist between sites.
stages.distribution: Margin and total distributions with larger sd than the regular season (margin sd assumed at about 14-16 per 40-48 minutes, an unsourced prior to be estimated); tie and overtime probabilities depend on format.

stages.name: Incentive state and schedule
stages.description: The tournament structure gives some games importance (seeding for the final) while others are for evaluation only, and schedule density in a short event affects rest decisions. The effect is on minutes and effort and varies across the week.
stages.distribution: State-dependent: effort and bench depth shift discretely between meaningful and meaningless games.

stages.name: Award selection for the event MVP
stages.description: The MVP contract is not a game outcome: the field of candidates is the handful of high-usage players who keep playing through the event, and the winner is usually on a team that reaches the final rounds. Shutdowns of top picks after a few games remove candidates abruptly, and voters weigh per-game scoring, draft status and team record; the choice is made from realised production, so each game day reshapes the field.
stages.distribution: Conditional choice over roughly 5-15 credible candidates with a long tail; probability mass concentrates fast after the first two game days and collapses for players who are shut down.

stages.name: Game and first-half margin and total distributions
stages.description: Game winner, spread and total and their first-half versions are read off one joint distribution of Summer League team points. The mean margin comes from translated roster strength weighted by who actually plays; the variance is far larger than in the NBA because of loose defense and fluid rotations. First halves are where drafted rookies and invited starters log most of their minutes, so the half margin tracks roster quality more closely, while second halves are handed to end-of-bench players and the margin regresses. The 1H winner adds an explicit tie outcome at integer margin zero.
stages.distribution: Approximately normal team-point totals with Summer-League-specific sd; margin pmf on integers with tie mass near 3-5% for halves; full-game margin wider and fat-tailed when one roster rests its prospects.

stages.name: Championship seeding and knockout path
stages.description: The champion contract is a path through the Las Vegas event: group-stage games produce a standings table in which ties are broken by tiebreakers including point differential, the top teams enter a single-elimination bracket and the rest play consolation games. Rosters thin as teams shut down prospects after qualification fails or after a few games, so a team's strength in the knockout is not its group-stage strength. Probability is the qualification probability times the knockout wins needed (two, semifinal and final, if the recent four-team knockout is kept; the 2026 format is unverified, see sl-format-facts), each close to a coin flip.
stages.distribution: Qualification is a discrete function of a four-game record plus margin tiebreak; title probability is a product of single-game win probabilities, heavily compressed toward 1/N by Summer League variance.

talent_strength.note: Translated player strength for those without NBA ratings.

opponent_matchup.note: With rosters assembled days before and few repeated opponents, matchup-specific scheme effects are not identifiable from Summer League history and add little beyond team strength and pace.

role_personnel.note: Minutes plans and who plays; the dominant signal.

availability_news.note: Game-day announcements and shutdown probabilities; no official report.

coaching_scheme.note: Coach evaluation philosophy and minutes policy.

environment.note: Arena conditions and the number of events (Las Vegas, California Classic, Utah) may matter through crowd and altitude (Salt Lake), but no input captures event-site effects and their size is unknown.

game_context_script.note: Importance state and format-specific scoring environment.

pace_volume.note: League-specific pace and possessions per game.

efficiency_conversion.note: Shooting efficiency regression for unfamiliar players is not addressed; the noise in efficiency of low-minutes rookies is large but no input models shrinkage to a talent prior beyond the translation prior.

distribution_variance.note: League-specific margin and total variance, plus the first-half share and tie mass for 1H contracts; the line-residual nba.score_resid is benchmark-only.

officiating_rules.note: Format and rules differences (period lengths, overtime, foul limits) captured as league baselines; officials' tendencies unmeasured.

settlement_contract.note: All eight series have rules: 1H winner tie strike and two-week postponement; game, spread and total texts silent on overtime; champion via bracket; MVP award with no co-winner rule.

nba.sl_talent_translation.label: Talent translation of rookies, two-way and G League players to a common Summer League strength scale
nba.sl_talent_translation.mechanism: Most Summer League minutes go to players without NBA data, so team strength must come from translating college, international and G League performance to an equivalent NBA-level rating.
nba.sl_talent_translation.rationale: A franchise's NBA rating says little about its Summer League roster; the strength is the minutes-weighted sum of translated player ratings, and uncertainty is large because translation factors are noisy.
nba.sl_talent_translation.measurement: For each player build a prior rating from available sources: college BPM/box-score composite (translation coefficient estimated historically by regressing NBA first-year BPM on college BPM with age and pace adjustments), G League per-minute production translated by a league-quality factor (about 0.6-0.7 estimated by backtest), international league adjustments; shrink to draft-slot prior (pick position mean) with prior weight 15 games-equivalent; team rating = minutes-weighted sum with expected minutes from announced rosters. As-of: roster announcement time.
raw_data: college and G League per-minute statistics, draft slot, age
NBA first-year BPM for translation sample
nba.sl_talent_translation.why: Replaces the unavailable NBA impact rating with a measurable prior for the players who actually play.

nba.sl_minutes_plan_hazard.label: Probability that a drafted player or returning rotation player plays, sits or is shut down
nba.sl_minutes_plan_hazard.mechanism: Summer League teams manage minutes for prospects and shut down players after a few games or when they are established; the probability a top prospect plays in a given game is a decision, not an injury process.
nba.sl_minutes_plan_hazard.rationale: The minutes a star rookie plays varies from full to zero by team policy, game number and announcements; the market impact is large because a top pick may account for a big share of team scoring.
nba.sl_minutes_plan_hazard.measurement: Part (a), historical: from Summer League box scores of the last 6 events build tables by draft-slot bucket (1-5, 6-14, 15-30, second round, undrafted, veteran), experience, and game number of P(plays) and the minutes distribution given plays; shutdown hazard after game k = logistic in previous-game minutes and slot. Part (b), forward only: capture timestamped announcements (will play, game-time, shut down) and map to realised participation; fit only after 2 events of capture and until then use part (a) alone and do not impute (b). Output P(plays) and minutes distribution; as-of: last announcement before the order time.
free_sources: Beat-writer announcements (X/Twitter, team websites), SOURCE_UNVERIFIED for archival access
raw_data: historical Summer League box scores with minutes by player
nba.sl_minutes_plan_hazard.why: Gives the structural distribution for the single largest Summer League uncertainty, whether the best player plays. Role lowered to secondary: the announcement half has no structured historical archive.

nba.sl_game_importance_incentive.label: Game importance and incentive state (tournament seeding, championship eligibility, evaluation goals)
nba.sl_game_importance_incentive.mechanism: Teams in Summer League care about evaluation and sometimes about the tournament; their minutes and effort depend on whether the game matters for seeding or the final.
nba.sl_game_importance_incentive.rationale: Win-maximizing effort is not the default: after a team is eliminated or clinched it plays deeper bench and evaluation lineups, which changes both the winner and the totals; the effect is predictable from the standings state.
nba.sl_game_importance_incentive.measurement: For each team and game compute leverage = P(team advances | win) - P(team advances | loss) from nba.sl_tournament_bracket_sim (standings, tiebreaks and remaining schedule as of the previous game), set to 0 for already-eliminated or already-clinched teams. Also record games played so far and back-to-back flag. Estimate the effect of leverage on starter minutes share and bench depth by regression over the last 5 events (team-game rows, event fixed effects, ridge shrinkage to zero with k=20 games). Output leverage and the expected shift in rotation minutes. As-of: after the previous game's final result.
free_sources: NBA.com Summer League standings and format pages
raw_data: standings and tournament rules by year
bench minutes in eliminated versus alive games
nba.sl_game_importance_incentive.why: Captures effort/rotation incentives that vary within the Summer League week and have no analog in the regular season.

nba.sl_format_scoring_baseline.label: Summer League-specific scoring, pace and margin variance baseline by format
nba.sl_format_scoring_baseline.mechanism: Summer League has a different game format (quarter length, overtime rule, fouling rules) and talent level, so scoring totals, pace and margin variance differ from the regular season and must be estimated from Summer League games.
nba.sl_format_scoring_baseline.rationale: Applying regular-season totals and margin sd to Summer League misstates both: games are typically higher scoring per possession with weaker defense and higher variance, so spread and total probabilities need league-specific parameters.
nba.sl_format_scoring_baseline.measurement: From all Summer League games over the last 5 events compute mean total, standard deviation of total and margin, tie-at-regulation frequency, OT frequency, and pace in possessions per 40 or 48 minutes depending on format; model margin as normal with sd by league (Las Vegas, California Classic, Salt Lake City) and shrink event-level sd to the pooled value (prior weight 30 games); update with games already played in the current event. As-of: games before tip. The game length L (40 or 48 minutes) and overtime procedure are read from the event's published rules and are unconfirmed (sl-format-facts); all rates are stored per minute and scaled by L, so no format value is hard-coded.
free_sources: nba_api summer league (leagueid 15), SOURCE_UNVERIFIED for coverage
raw_data: game results, period scores, possessions, event identifiers
published event rules (game length, overtime procedure)
nba.sl_format_scoring_baseline.why: Provides correct variance and totals scale for spread and total contracts in a league with little history.

nba.sl_mvp_award_model.label: Summer League MVP candidate model: individual production share, team advancement and games played
nba.sl_mvp_award_model.mechanism: The Summer League MVP goes to a player who combines a high scoring and usage share with a team that advances, and who plays most of his team's games; a candidate's chance is a conditional choice among the event's leading producers, weighted by his team's path to the final.
nba.sl_mvp_award_model.rationale: No other input gives an award outcome: team strength and game inputs price games, while the award depends on who plays enough games, per-game production relative to the field and voter emphasis on draft status and team success. Subtle: top picks often play two or three games and are shut down, so expected games played, not talent, is the first filter.
nba.sl_mvp_award_model.measurement: Step 1: for each candidate, expected games played = sum over the team's scheduled games of P(plays) from nba.sl_minutes_plan_hazard, and expected points and usage per game from nba.sl_talent_translation and nba.sl_format_scoring_baseline. Step 2: team advancement probability from simulated event standings and the knockout. Step 3: conditional logit over candidates with covariates (expected total points, usage rank, team reaches the final, draft slot) fitted on past Summer League MVP winners and runners-up (at least 10 events, ridge penalty, prior weight 5 events). Step 4: renormalise across candidates; update after each game day with realised production. As-of: start of the event, then nightly.
free_sources: NBA.com Summer League stats and award announcements (free)
Basketball-Reference Summer League pages (free, polite scraping; coverage by year unverified)
raw_data: Summer League player box scores by game
past Summer League MVP winners and finalists with team results
nba.sl_mvp_award_model.why: KXNBASUMMERMVP is the only rules-verified series in this archetype and had no input; the award depends on games played, production share and team advancement.

nba.sl_first_half_share.label: Summer League first-half share of team points and margin by roster composition
nba.sl_first_half_share.mechanism: Summer League coaches give prospects and invited starters most first-half minutes and hand the second half to fringe players, so first-half points and margin depend more on top-of-roster strength than the full game.
nba.sl_first_half_share.rationale: First-half spread, total and winner contracts need the half distribution, not half the game distribution: the half margin carries a larger share of the roster-strength signal, its variance is not half the game variance, and the tie mass at zero is priced by KXNBASUMMER1HWINNER directly.
nba.sl_first_half_share.measurement: From the last five Summer League events compute, per game and team, first-half points / game points and first-half margin / game margin; regress the first-half margin on the minutes-weighted translated strength of the players who logged first-half minutes (from play-by-play substitutions) versus the full-game weighted strength; report the first-half share of mean total (shrunk to the pooled value with prior weight 40 games), the half-margin sd and the empirical integer tie frequency of first halves. As-of: pre-tip, using announced participation.
free_sources: NBA.com Summer League box scores and period scores
nba_api play-by-play for Summer League games (league id for Summer League)
raw_data: Summer League period scores by game
nba.sl_first_half_share.why: Prices KXNBASUMMER1HSPREAD, KXNBASUMMER1HTOTAL and KXNBASUMMER1HWINNER, which settle on first-half points only and whose margin is driven by the prospects who play first-half minutes.

nba.sl_tournament_bracket_sim.label: Summer League tournament standings, tiebreak and knockout simulation
nba.sl_tournament_bracket_sim.mechanism: The Summer League champion is the winner of a knockout among the top teams of the group stage; qualification depends on a short record and a point-differential tiebreak, and later rounds are single games.
nba.sl_tournament_bracket_sim.rationale: With four group games per team, ties in record are common and point differential decides qualification, so a team's title chance depends on margin as well as wins; rosters also change between stages as prospects are shut down, so the knockout strength must be re-estimated, not carried over.
nba.sl_tournament_bracket_sim.measurement: Encode the current event format (group games per team, number of knockout qualifiers, tiebreak order including point differential) from the league's published rules; simulate remaining group games from the game-level margin distribution (nba.sl_format_scoring_baseline with team means from nba.sl_talent_translation and participation from nba.sl_minutes_plan_hazard), apply the tiebreaks, then simulate the bracket with per-round strength that drops by the expected shutdown share; 20,000 paths; output P(qualify), P(reach final), P(champion). As-of: after each game day.
free_sources: NBA.com Summer League standings and format page
nba.sl_tournament_bracket_sim.why: Gives the qualification and knockout path that KXNBASUMMER settles on; the archetype otherwise had no input for the bracket or its margin-based tiebreak.

nba.summer_league_minutes.reason: Who plays and how many minutes each gets is the entire strength signal in Summer League; but it is a bundle (roster, minutes plans, rookie usage) with no measurement protocol and information arrives on game day.

nba.player_impact.reason: Prior impact ratings work only for returning NBA rotation players; most Summer League minutes go to rookies, two-way and G League players for whom an NBA impact metric does not exist.

nba.injuries_pit.reason: There is no official injury report for Summer League in the NBA format; availability is announced informally (team beat writers, social posts), so the vintage-based official-report framing does not apply.

nba.pace.reason: League-specific pace and scoring baselines differ from the regular season because of format and rosters; useful only as a Summer League-specific estimate, not NBA team pace.

nba.score_resid.reason: Residual relative to market lines is a calibration of the book and has little Summer League history; the required object is the raw distribution of Summer League margins and totals.

nba.rest_travel.reason: Back-to-back and short-turnaround schedule density in Las Vegas affects rest decisions for prospects; secondary to the minutes plan itself.

nba.news.reason: Demoted from primary: roster announcements and shutdown news are the key game-day information, but there is no structured historical archive of them (sl-announcement-data), so no calibrated map can be built until live capture is run; the label also lumps in trades and coaching news.

nba.rotation.reason: Coach minutes plans (equal-time evaluation, rookie caps) override win-maximizing rotations; the structure differs from the regular season and history is thin.

m.quote_history.reason: Price path reveals information arrival, not game outcomes; thin Summer League markets make it noisy.

m.rules_text.reason: Only KXNBASUMMERMVP has rules text; Summer League game rules (shorter quarters, overtime format, tournament tiebreaks) differ from the NBA and the game contracts' treatment of them is unread, so capturing the rules remains primary.

m.external_lines.reason: The attached reason refers to sportsbook futures; for game markets lines are benchmarks, and Summer League books are known to be thinner and less efficient, so copying them is risky.

interactions.mechanism: Team strength is the minutes-weighted sum of player ratings, so the same rating matters more for a player with 28 expected minutes than one with 10; a top pick who is shut down removes both his rating and the minutes, producing a step in team strength rather than a gradual change.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare team margin with and without the top-drafted player across past Summer Leagues, controlling for opponent.

interactions.mechanism: Summer League totals are both higher-variance and higher-pace than regular-season; the variance of totals scales with possessions and with defensive looseness, so the sd of total and sd of margin move together with the format baseline.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate total and margin sd by event and format from past Summer League results and test heteroskedasticity versus pace.

interactions.mechanism: A late announcement that a key rookie rests switches the team to a different regime (bench-heavy rotation, evaluation lineups); the market reaction depends on timing, and the same news before and after the order time has different value.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare the move in team margin conditional on announcement timestamps relative to the prior price time.

interactions.mechanism: Importance and schedule density jointly determine who rests: on the second game of a back-to-back with no seeding stakes, minutes shift to bench and prospects, whereas the same schedule in a must-win game keeps starters; the effect of rest depends on stakes.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress minutes of top prospects on back-to-back x importance indicator across past events.

interactions.mechanism: A candidate's MVP chance is roughly P(keeps playing) times P(chosen | plays through), so a top pick with the best per-game production can be a poor MVP bet if his team plans a two-game appearance, while a second-year player on a contending roster gains; the shutdown hazard multiplies the whole award probability.
interactions.how_to_test: On past events compare MVP winners' games played with the field's top scorers per game; fit the award logit with and without expected games played.

interactions.mechanism: When a team's top prospect is announced out, the first-half margin loses most of its roster-strength signal while the full-game margin changes less, because the second half was going to fringe players anyway; first-half contracts react more to participation news than game contracts.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare first-half and full-game margin residuals in games where a top-10 pick sat versus played, over five Summer League events.

nonlinearities.shape: bimodal/step: top prospects play full or not at all
nonlinearities.why: The impact of a top pick on team strength is not proportional to expected minutes because the distribution is bimodal; mean-minutes models understate the variance of team strength and the effect of announcements.

nonlinearities.shape: heavy-tailed star effect: team strength is dominated by one or two high-talent players
nonlinearities.why: Summer League rosters contain few players above NBA-rotation level and their share of usage is large, so team strength is convex in the top player's rating.

nonlinearities.shape: heteroskedastic: margin sd larger in blowout-prone mismatches and in loose-defense formats
nonlinearities.why: Summer League games have higher variance than regular-season games and variance grows with talent gaps, so the format baseline's margin sd must be heteroskedastic in the talent gap; normal approximations with a fixed sd misprice tails.

contract.settlement_definition: KXNBATEAMTOTAL is a binary over/under on one named team's points in the named game: YES if the team scores more than the half-point strike (floor_strike 135.5, strike_type greater, so no push). A game postponed but starting within 48 hours stays open and resolves on the official final result; a game cancelled or not started within 48 hours resolves all markets at a fair price. The sampled rules do not say whether overtime points count, so the OT inclusion that the existing draft asserts is not verified; the ledger has only one series for this archetype.

rules_evidence.quote: If Oklahoma City scores more than 135.5 points in the Oklahoma City vs Memphis Pro Basketball game originally scheduled for Nov 6, 2026, then the market resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: Strike construction: 'more than X.5' on one team's points in the whole game, so no push and a single-team count.

rules_evidence.quote: If the game is postponed but begins within 48 hours of its originally scheduled start time, the market will remain open and resolve based on the official final result.
rules_evidence.establishes: Postponement within 48 hours keeps the market open and uses the official final result.

rules_evidence.quote: If the game is cancelled or not started within 48 hours of its originally scheduled start, all markets will resolve to a fair price.
rules_evidence.establishes: Cancellation or long delay voids at a fair price, not NO.

variants_and_edge_cases: Overtime: the sampled primary and secondary text never mention overtime; 'the official final result' of a game normally includes OT points, which would add roughly 11-13 points to each team in about 6% of games, but this is unverified and changes tail probabilities.

Strike construction: the sampled strike of 135.5 for Oklahoma City is well above a typical team total (about 115-120), consistent with a ladder of rungs; the contract is a single threshold per market with no push at half-point strikes.

Team total is not a function of a single team's offense: it depends on the shared possession count and the opponent's play, so correlated markets (game total, spread, opponent team total) must be internally consistent.
Void on cancellation or a delay beyond 48 hours pays a fair price, so late-season games affected by weather or travel have no NO risk but no information either.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official final score of the game as published by the league; the sampled rules refer to 'the official final result' without naming a provider.

mechanism.summary: A team's points equal the shared number of possessions times its points per possession, plus overtime if counted. Possessions are a joint property of both teams (the slower style may dominate, a hypothesis to be tested), while points per possession come from the matchup of own offense with the opponent's defense decomposed into shooting, turnovers, offensive rebounds and free throws, with tonight's availability changing every factor. Game script then bends the result: a favorite's points flatten in garbage time, an underdog's rise from late fouling and deep-bench scoring, so team points are a nonlinear function of expected margin. Variance depends on style (three-point reliance, pace) and is large relative to strike spacing, and the settlement wording on overtime determines whether a 6% mixture component of about a dozen points is part of the distribution.

stages.name: Shared possessions
stages.description: The game's possession count is one number determined jointly by both teams' tempo preferences, transition rates and turnovers; averaging the two teams' season paces misstates it, since the slower style may dominate (hypothesis, not established). Lineup changes (a missing point guard) shift tempo for the whole game.
stages.distribution: Roughly normal with mean near 98-100 and sd 4-5 possessions; a right skew from OT; correlated with both teams' scoring.

stages.name: Own offense against the opponent's defense
stages.description: Points per possession depend on own shot quality, turnover and offensive rebound tendencies, free throws and the opponent's defensive profile in each factor. The additive offensive-minus-defensive rating approximates this but the factor decomposition handles scheme-specific deviations such as a rim-heavy offense against a drop defense.
stages.distribution: Efficiency per 100 possessions with sd across teams of about 4; matchup deviations of 1-2 points; per-game noise dominated by three-point variance.

stages.name: Availability and unit changes
stages.description: Absence of own scorers lowers offensive rating and also changes pace; absence of the opponent's rim protector or point-of-attack defender raises it. Starters are confirmed shortly before tip and rotation changes alter the expected minutes of the best units.
stages.distribution: Discrete personnel states with rating shifts of 1-5 points per 100 possessions per key absence.

stages.name: Shooting variance and free throws
stages.description: Single-game three-point shooting luck of both teams, and the foul-and-free-throw environment (crew tendencies, bonus), are the largest random components of points; they regress to expectation between games and have style-dependent variance. Free throws contribute 3-4 points per game across crews.
stages.distribution: Team points sd about 11-14, larger for three-point-reliant teams; shooting shocks are positively correlated between the two teams' totals through pace.

stages.name: Game script and overtime
stages.description: Win probability bends team points: favorites' starters sit in garbage time, underdogs score late through fouling and bench possessions; the mapping from expected margin to team points is nonlinear. Overtime, if counted, adds a mixture component of about a dozen points with probability near 6%.
stages.distribution: Skewed conditional distribution; mixture with an OT component whose size is about 11-13 points and weight about 5-7%.

stages.name: Settlement
stages.description: Settlement is the official final score for the named team above a half-point strike; cancellation and long delays void at a fair price. The sampled rules do not say whether overtime counts, which is the largest unknown.
stages.distribution: Binary indicator on integer points; no push.

talent_strength.note: Team offense and opponent defense, opponent-adjusted and decomposed.

role_personnel.note: Who plays tonight; usage redistribution is weak at the team level.

availability_news.note: Own and opponent absences with vintage.

coaching_scheme.note: Tempo and shot-selection styles of both coaches.

environment.note: Altitude (Denver, Utah), arena shooting backdrop and travel effects on scoring are not represented by any input of this archetype; the effect on team points is small but systematic for specific venues.

efficiency_conversion.note: Efficiency per possession and luck regression.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Back-to-back, schedule density and late-season rest decisions affect scoring through energy and minutes, but no input of this archetype represents them; the size at the team-total level is unquantified.

officiating_rules.note: Crew foul-call tendency and team free-throw rate.

settlement_contract.note: Strike construction, postponement and void; OT treatment unknown.

nba.four_factors_matchup.label: Expected four factors for own offense vs opponent defense (eFG%, turnover rate, offensive rebound rate, free-throw rate)
nba.four_factors_matchup.mechanism: Team points per possession decompose into shooting efficiency, turnovers, offensive rebounds and free-throw rate; each factor responds to the specific opponent differently than the overall rating does.
nba.four_factors_matchup.rationale: Offensive rating against defensive rating is an additive approximation; a rim-heavy offense against a drop defense, or a turnover-prone offense against a pressure defense, deviates from it, and the factor-level decomposition allows shot profile, scheme and luck to enter in the right place.
nba.four_factors_matchup.measurement: For each team compute offensive and defensive four factors per 100 possessions over last 25 games (half-life 12) and season, opponent-adjusted by the standard iterative method; expected eFG = league + (own offense - league) + (opp defense allowed - league) with team-specific shrinkage weights (prior weight 20 games); combine factors into expected points per 100 using regression weights (eFG about 0.4, TOV 0.25, ORB 0.2, FT 0.15). As-of: games before tip, with lineup adjustments for absentees.
raw_data: Team game box scores: FGM, FG3M, FGA, TOV, OREB, FTA, possessions
nba.four_factors_matchup.why: Allows each of shot-quality, turnover pressure and free-throw rate to differ by opponent; matches the contract's single-team scoring.

nba.joint_pace_interaction.label: Joint matchup pace from both teams' pace preferences (slower-team weight and transition vs half-court)
nba.joint_pace_interaction.mechanism: Game possessions are one shared number whose expectation is not the average of two teams' paces; a hypothesis to test is that the slower style dominates and transition-heavy teams are constrained by opponent turnovers and rebounds.
nba.joint_pace_interaction.rationale: A team's total depends on the shared possession count, so error in the pace of the matchup translates directly into points; averaging season paces misstates a matchup of a fast team vs a slow team.
nba.joint_pace_interaction.measurement: From 5 seasons of games regress game possessions on both teams' season paces (adjusted for home), their interaction and style flags (transition share, post-up share) to get weights (the weight on the slower team is a free parameter to be estimated; 0.55 is only an illustrative value, not a finding); add lineup adjustment from projected starters; residual sd by matchup type (fast-fast, fast-slow). Output expected possessions and sd. As-of: tip.
nba.joint_pace_interaction.why: Gives the correct possession count for the matchup rather than a single-team pace.

nba.team_points_variance_by_style.label: Style-dependent variance of a team's points (three-point reliance, transition share, pace)
nba.team_points_variance_by_style.mechanism: Teams that take many threes and play fast have higher game-to-game variance in points than slow half-court teams; the over/under probability at a given strike depends on the sd, not only the mean.
nba.team_points_variance_by_style.rationale: A team total strike near the mean has probability near 50% regardless of variance, but strikes at 5-10 points away depend on the sd; the sd is team- and matchup-specific and is typically 11-14 points.
nba.team_points_variance_by_style.measurement: Compute each team's residual sd of points (actual minus rating-based expectation, no market lines) over a season with regression on three-point attempt rate, pace and opponent style; shrink to league sd (about 12.5) with prior weight 25 games; combine own sd and opponent style effects; model the points distribution as skew-normal with skew from blowout probability. As-of: games before tip. Also output tail quantiles of own team points (80th, 90th, 95th and 99th percentile) and P(points >= strike) at strikes far above the mean, separately for a regulation-only and an overtime-included version, because far-away strikes (such as 135.5) are priced by the tail (three-point shooting variance, overtime) and not by the mean.
nba.team_points_variance_by_style.why: Provides the shape parameter needed to price strikes away from the mean and the asymmetry of tails. Strikes far above the team mean (tt-strike-ladder) make the upper tail, not the sd, the quantity to estimate.

nba.team_points_margin_curve.label: Expected team points as a function of the game's expected margin (winner-loser asymmetry and garbage-time shape)
nba.team_points_margin_curve.mechanism: A team's points are not linear in the expected margin: favorites' points flatten (garbage time) and underdogs gain late points through fouling and deep-bench scoring, so the mapping from win probability to team points is a curve.
nba.team_points_margin_curve.rationale: Deriving team totals as (total ± spread)/2 assumes linearity; the empirical curve can differ by 1-2 points at large spreads, and this matters for strikes in a market keyed to the team's own points.
nba.team_points_margin_curve.measurement: From 5 seasons of games compute realised team points minus rating-based expected points as a function of pregame expected margin built from ratings (not the spread) in bins of 2 points; fit a monotone-spline of own points on expected margin with total environment as a covariate; use leave-one-season-out cross-validation; output expected team points given expected margin and total. Vintage rule: every team rating used (nba.off_rtg, nba.def_rtg, nba.lineup_adj_rating) must be the snapshot computed from games completed before that historical game's tipoff, stored daily over the 5 seasons, with the confirmed-inactive adjustment as of the pregame report; end-of-season or later-revised ratings are not allowed, as they leak the game's own result.
free_sources: Computed from nba_api game logs and team ratings
raw_data: team-game points, pregame expected margin from as-of ratings (5 seasons)
nba.team_points_margin_curve.why: Replaces the benchmark-derived implied team total with a market-free curve.

nba.rating_blowout_minutes_curve.label: Ratings-based blowout probability and starter-minutes-vs-margin curve (market-free)
nba.rating_blowout_minutes_curve.mechanism: Rebuilds the blowout risk from team strength and rotation history instead of the closing spread: a ratings-implied expected margin and margin spread give P(large lead), and a coach/player minutes-versus-margin curve converts each margin path into expected minutes lost by starters and gained by bench players.
nba.rating_blowout_minutes_curve.rationale: The catalog input nba.garbage is defined from the closing spread, which is a market price and so a benchmark, not an input. The causal quantity is the chance that the margin passes the coach's pull threshold early enough to matter, and how much playing time each player then loses. Subtle: the loss depends on when the lead arrives (a 20-point lead entering Q4 removes far more starter minutes than one reached with 3 minutes left), on the coach, and on whether the trailing team also pulls starters, so the curve must be conditional on the margin path and not only on the final margin.
nba.rating_blowout_minutes_curve.measurement: Step 1, expected margin: mu = (NetRtg_home_adj - NetRtg_away_adj) * expected_possessions/100 + home_adv, where NetRtg_adj is the as-of-tipoff opponent-adjusted net rating from nba.off_rtg and nba.def_rtg (ridge regression on game point differential, half-life about 25 games, shrunk to the preseason prior with n_prior about 20 games as a placeholder to be fitted), adjusted for the confirmed unavailable players via nba.lineup_adj_rating, home_adv fitted on the last 5 seasons (about 2 points). Step 2, margin spread: sd_margin fitted on 5 seasons of residuals of final margin versus mu (league-wide roughly 12-13 points, to be estimated, with a heavier empirical tail than normal). Step 3: P(final |margin| >= 15/20/25) and P(|lead| >= 15/20 entering Q4) from the empirical residual distribution around mu. Step 4, minutes curve: from play-by-play stints, per team-season, expected minutes of each rotation player conditional on margin entering Q4 in bins (0-9, 10-14, 15-19, 20+), shrunk toward the league curve with k about 30 blowout games. Output per player: expected minutes lost and the probability of falling below a stated minutes level. No closing line or other price is used; the spread is retained only to benchmark calibration of step 3.

Basketball-Reference game logs and play-by-play (free, polite scraping)
nba.rating_blowout_minutes_curve.why: Team scoring above a high strike needs full-strength lineups late, and the winning team sits starters while the losing team may not; the curve gives both sides without the spread.
raw_data: team-game final margins and opponent-adjusted ratings as of tipoff (5 seasons)
play-by-play substitution stints with margin entering Q4

nba.ot_prob_ratings_margin.label: Market-free overtime probability and overtime scoring increment from the ratings-implied regulation margin
nba.ot_prob_ratings_margin.mechanism: A game goes to overtime only if the regulation margin is exactly zero, so P(OT) is the mass at zero of the regulation-margin distribution, highest for evenly matched teams; each five-minute overtime then adds scoring at both teams' per-minute rates, and a further overtime follows with the tie probability of a five-minute period.
nba.ot_prob_ratings_margin.rationale: The catalog nba.ot_model conditions P(OT) on the closing-spread bucket (a market quantity) and says one OT adds about 10-12 points to totals, which is the per-team figure, not the combined one. A market-free version takes the regulation-margin distribution from team ratings and sizes OT correctly: roughly 11-13 points per team and 22-26 combined per period, with repeated overtimes possible. Subtle: the zero-margin mass is larger than a continuous normal approximation gives, because end-of-game tactics (holding for the last shot, fouling when ahead by three) cluster regulation margins between 0 and 3.
nba.ot_prob_ratings_margin.measurement: Step 1: regulation-margin mean mu from nba.rating_blowout_minutes_curve (opponent-adjusted net ratings x expected possessions/100 + home advantage, as of tipoff, adjusted for confirmed inactives). Step 2: P(regulation tie) = logistic regression of the indicator "regulation margin = 0" on |mu| over the last 5 regular seasons (about 6,000 games; league base rate to be estimated), smoothed across 1-point |mu| bins. Step 3: per-team OT points = league points per team per OT period from play-by-play scaled by the team's opponent-adjusted pace and offensive rating relative to league; combined OT points = sum over both teams. Step 4: P(k-th OT | (k-1)-th OT) = pooled empirical tie rate of five-minute periods with prior weight 200 OT periods. Output P(OT), P(2+ OT), per-team and combined OT-points distributions. Only team ratings, pace and results enter.

Basketball-Reference box scores with OT period lines (free, polite scraping)

nba.ot_prob_ratings_margin.why: If OT counts toward the official final result, a team adds roughly 11-13 points in about 6% of games, more for evenly matched games; the ratings-implied zero-margin mass gives that weight without a closing spread.

nba.off_rtg.reason: Own offense per 100 possessions is the main driver of team points; must be opponent-adjusted and unit-aware, and a single season average is slow to react to rotation changes.

nba.def_rtg.reason: Opponent defense enters through points allowed per possession; defensive ratings are noisier than offensive ones and their interaction with the offense's shot profile is not additive.

nba.pace.reason: Possessions are a joint property of both teams; the label says 'own possessions', which misstates the mechanism: only the game's shared possession count exists, and the slower team's style tends to dominate.

nba.implied_team_totals.reason: Derived from the sportsbook spread and total; it is the market's price for this very contract, so labelled primary it would make a model equal to the market; keep only for the consistency check.

nba.lineup_adj_rating.reason: Tonight's active set changes offense by several points per 100; essential, but 'availability-adjusted offense' needs lineup-specific offense/defense separation rather than a single net rating.

nba.injuries_pit.reason: Own scorers and opponent rim protectors both move expected points; vintage matters because starters are confirmed shortly before tip.

nba.usage.reason: Usage redistribution among own players changes who scores but barely changes team points; the existing text says as much, so this belongs as context for player markets rather than a team-total driver.

nba.shot_profile.reason: Own shot mix against the opponent's allowed mix sets expected efficiency; stable and the basis for the four-factors expectation.

nba.three_pt_luck.reason: Own and opponent 3P% regression matters for forecasting team points from recent results; effect modest per game but the main reason recent point totals mislead.

nba.fouls_ft.reason: Free-throw rate and crew foul tendency change points from the line (about 3-4 points per game across crews); must be combined with game script because trailing teams foul more.

nba.garbage.reason: Catalog definition is "blowout probability from spread", a closing-line quantity, so it is a market benchmark and not an input. Removed from stages, coverage, interactions and data feeds; replaced by the market-free nba.rating_blowout_minutes_curve built from ratings and rotation history. Prior note: Garbage time lowers the favorite's points while the underdog scores against bench units and via late fouls; sign differs by team, so this is the key skew input; rebuilt from ratings, not the spread.

nba.ot_model.reason: Catalog measurement bins P(OT) by |spread| and total buckets (closing-line quantities), so as defined it is market-derived and a benchmark; it also states OT adds about 10-12 points to totals, which is the per-team figure (combined is about 22-26). Replaced in stages, coverage, interactions, nonlinearities and feeds by the market-free nba.ot_prob_ratings_margin.

m.quote_history.reason: Price path measures information arrival rather than points; useful for timing only.

m.rules_text.reason: The sampled rules are silent on overtime for team totals, so the settlement wording is a key unknown; the existing note that OT is 'included per rules text' is not supported by the sampled text.

m.external_lines.reason: Labelled primary but a sportsbook team-total line is the benchmark to beat, not an input.

m.ladder_structure.reason: Coherence of team total, game total and spread is an arbitrage check among market prices; not a driver.

nba.market_calibration_bias.reason: Price-bucket bias in the Kalshi book; overlay on model probabilities.

m.volume_oi.reason: Open interest has no link to points scored; liquidity is driven by team popularity.

m.trade_tape.reason: Order flow is microstructure and carries no information about the scoring process.

m.settlement_truth.reason: Settled values are labels; reconcile with official final scores including how OT is handled.

interactions.mechanism: Own efficiency against this defense depends on factor-level fit: a rim-heavy offense gains against a drop defense that concedes rim attempts, but loses against one that walls the paint; the additive rating difference averages these opposite cases and so errs systematically for extreme styles.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare error of additive rating prediction versus the four-factor matchup prediction for teams in the top and bottom rim-rate quintiles.

interactions.mechanism: The favorite's expected points flatten when the game becomes lopsided because starters sit while the underdog's points keep rising through late fouls and bench scoring; the relation of team points to margin is piecewise with a kink around a 10-12 point expected margin.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit a spline of own points on expected margin using ratings and check for the kink separately for favorites and underdogs.

interactions.mechanism: A missing ball handler lowers both team efficiency and the possession count; the two effects multiply in the points total so a model that adjusts only the rating understates the points drop, and the opponent's points move too through the shared pace.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare team points and possessions in games without the primary handler versus with, controlling for opponent.

interactions.mechanism: Trailing teams foul late and the leading team shoots the free throws, so crew foul tendency raises the favorite's points more in close games and the underdog's points via fouls drawn in garbage time; effect depends on the margin path.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate FT points by team and margin bin, interacted with crew foul rate.

interactions.mechanism: A three-point-reliant team has high variance in points, so strikes far from the mean have probability much different from a low-variance team; luck regression (the three-point mean) and variance (the dispersion) are separate parameters that both matter for strike distance.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare calibration of P(over) at strikes 6+ points from the mean using team-specific versus pooled variance.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold with asymmetric effect on favorite and underdog
nonlinearities.why: Beyond about a 15-point margin late, starters sit and the favorite's points fall, while the underdog's points rise slightly; the relation is not monotone in blowout probability and differs by side.

nonlinearities.shape: mixture step: about 6% probability of adding roughly a dozen points if OT counts
nonlinearities.why: The team-points distribution acquires a right-hand lump from OT; the over probability for high strikes is lifted by the mixture while the central probability is nearly unaffected.

nonlinearities.shape: concave in possession count for points: efficiency declines as pace increases
nonlinearities.why: Faster pace raises possessions but lowers per-possession efficiency slightly (quicker shots), so points rise less than proportionally with pace.
